q: By default, a newly created storage account accepts connections from:
opts: Only the VNet it was created in
exp: New storage accounts are reachable from all networks by default (public network access is enabled), although every request still needs valid authorisation. You restrict this afterwards with the firewall (selected networks), private endpoints, or by disabling public network access.

q: Which CLI command adds a VNet subnet rule to a storage account firewall?
opts: az storage account network-rule add --account-name st1 --vnet-name VNet1 --subnet SubnetA
az network vnet rule add --storage st1
exp: az storage account network-rule add adds a firewall rule to a storage account. Use --vnet-name and --subnet for a virtual network rule, or --ip-address for a public IP rule. The subnet also needs the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint. The other commands don't exist.

q: After enabling the firewall with selected networks, an admin can't browse containers in the portal from home. Their data access works from Azure VMs. Why?
opts: The portal requests come from the admin's public IP, which isn't in the IP rules
exp: When you browse data in the portal, the requests come from your browser, so the storage account sees your home or office public IP. If that IP isn't in the firewall's IP rules, data browsing fails even though the account settings still load. VMs in an allowed subnet work because their traffic matches the VNet rule.

q: Can you add a private IP range (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8) to the storage firewall's IP rules to allow on-premises clients?
opts: No — IP rules accept public IP addresses only; use VNet rules or private endpoints for private ranges
exp: Storage firewall IP rules accept only public internet addresses. Private ranges such as 10.0.0.0/8 aren't allowed, because requests from on-premises reach Azure from a public IP. For private connectivity from on-premises, use a private endpoint reached over VPN or ExpressRoute.

q: A subnet in a different region from the storage account must be allowed by a VNet rule. What applies?
opts: It's supported: VNet rules can allow subnets in other regions
Must peer the VNet with the storage account
exp: Storage service endpoints work across regions, so a VNet rule can allow a subnet in a different region from the storage account. You don't need ZRS or peering for this. Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on that subnet and add the VNet rule.

q: A storage account needs a private endpoint for both blob and file access. How many private endpoints are required?
opts: Two — one per sub-resource (blob and file)
None; one service endpoint covers both
exp: A storage private endpoint connects to one sub-resource (service): blob, file, queue, table, web or dfs. To reach both blob and file privately you need two private endpoints, each with its own private DNS zone (privatelink.blob… and privatelink.file…). Service endpoints are a different feature.

q: Which private DNS zone name is used for blob private endpoints?
exp: Blob private endpoints use the private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net. The public name contosodata.blob.core.windows.net becomes a CNAME to contosodata.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, which this zone resolves to the private IP. Each service has its own privatelink zone.

q: You create a private endpoint and want to block all public internet access to the storage account. Which setting?
exp: Setting public network access to Disabled blocks every request that doesn't come through a private endpoint, including from the internet. 'Allow trusted services' is an exception for some Azure services, while secure transfer and minimum TLS control encryption in transit, not which networks can connect.

q: Which TWO statements about a storage private endpoint are true?
opts: It consumes a private IP from your VNet subnet
It works from on-premises over VPN or ExpressRoute
It requires a service endpoint on the same subnet
It makes the account publicly readable
exp: Private endpoints get a VNet IP and are reachable from connected networks. They don't require a service endpoint.

q: What does 'Secure transfer required' do on a storage account?
opts: Rejects requests made over HTTP (and SMB without encryption)
exp: 'Secure transfer required' makes the account reject requests over plain HTTP and SMB connections without encryption, so data is always encrypted in transit. It doesn't control encryption at rest (that's always on), private endpoints or MFA.

q: Security policy says clients must use TLS 1.2 or later. Which storage setting?
exp: The minimum TLS version setting on a storage account rejects requests that use older TLS, so setting it to TLS 1.2 blocks TLS 1.0 and 1.1 clients. Turning secure transfer off would allow plain HTTP, which is the opposite of what's needed, and the other options aren't about TLS.

q: Which SAS type can grant access to multiple services (blob, file, queue, table) in a single token?
exp: An account SAS is signed with the account key and can cover several services (blob, file, queue and table) and service-level operations in one token. A service SAS covers only one service, a user delegation SAS can't span services, and a stored access policy isn't a SAS type.

q: In a SAS URL, which parameter holds the expiry time?
exp: In a SAS URL, se is the signed expiry time. sp holds the permissions, sv the storage service version, st the start time, and sig the signature that proves the token is genuine.

q: In a SAS URL, 'sp=rl' means:
exp: The sp parameter lists the permissions the SAS grants: r = read, l = list, w = write, d = delete, c = create, a = add. sp=rl therefore allows reading blobs and listing them, but not writing or deleting.

q: Security requires blocking all SAS signed with account keys while still allowing Entra-based access. What do you configure?
opts: Disable 'Allow storage account key access' (shared key authorization)
exp: Disabling shared key authorization blocks account keys, account SAS, and service SAS. User delegation SAS (Entra) still works.

q: What is the maximum validity of a user delegation SAS?
opts: 7 days (limited by the user delegation key)
exp: A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key, which is valid for at most 7 days. The SAS can't outlive the key, so 7 days is the maximum. Account and service SAS don't have this limit, which is one reason they're riskier.

q: Which CLI command generates a SAS for a single blob?
exp: az storage blob generate-sas creates a SAS for one blob, with options for permissions, expiry, IP range and protocol. az storage account keys list returns the account keys, not a SAS. The other commands don't exist.

q: A SAS token works in testing, then fails for a partner a week later with 403 errors. Which is the most likely cause?
opts: The SAS expired (se passed) or the signing key was rotated
exp: A SAS that worked and later returns 403 has most often expired (its se time has passed) or was invalidated because the key that signed it was regenerated. Other causes are IP or protocol limits and firewall rules. The tier and archiving don't produce authorisation errors on valid SAS tokens.

q: Which levels can have a stored access policy?
exp: Stored access policies are defined on a container, a file share, a queue or a table, and service SAS tokens for that resource can reference them. They can't be set on a whole storage account, on a single blob, or anywhere outside storage.

q: A SAS references stored access policy 'p1'. You delete p1 and create a new policy with the same name 'p1'. What happens to the old SAS?
opts: It becomes valid again under the new p1's settings
exp: SAS tokens reference the policy by name. Recreating the same name re-associates them, so use new names when revoking.

q: How long can it take for a change to a stored access policy to take effect?
exp: After you create, change or delete a stored access policy, it can take up to 30 seconds to take effect. During that time SAS tokens linked to the policy may still behave according to the old settings.

q: Order the steps to rotate storage account keys with no downtime:
items: Update applications back to key1 (new value)
exp: Move the applications to key2 first, so key1 is no longer in use. Regenerate key1 safely, switch the applications to the new key1, and then regenerate key2. At every step the applications have a valid key, so nothing goes down.

q: Which CLI command regenerates the primary storage key?
opts: az storage account keys renew --account-name st1 --key primary
exp: az storage account keys renew --key primary (or secondary) regenerates one of the two account keys. Any SAS signed with the old key stops working. az keyvault key rotate rotates keys stored in Key Vault, not storage account keys.

q: Which role lets a user list storage account access keys?
opts: Storage Account Key Operator Service Role (or Contributor/Owner)
exp: Listing keys requires Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listkeys/action, which roles like Storage Account Key Operator Service Role and Contributor include.

q: What does a key expiration policy on a storage account do?
opts: Flags keys that are older than the set interval (in Azure Policy/Advisor) so you know to rotate them
exp: A key expiration policy sets how often the account keys should be rotated (for example, every 90 days). Azure doesn't rotate the keys for you; overdue keys are flagged so you can rotate them, and you can audit this with Azure Policy. It doesn't delete keys or block SAS.

q: An app must upload and delete blobs using its managed identity. Least-privilege role?
exp: Storage Blob Data Contributor allows reading, writing and deleting blob data, which is exactly what the app needs. Storage Blob Data Owner also manages POSIX ACLs on Data Lake, which is more than required. Contributor and Storage Account Contributor are control-plane roles that don't grant data access directly.

q: A user must manage POSIX ACLs on a Data Lake Storage Gen2 account. Which role?
exp: On Data Lake Storage Gen2 (hierarchical namespace), only Storage Blob Data Owner, or the owning user of a file or directory, can set ownership and change POSIX access control lists. Storage Blob Data Contributor can read and write data but can't manage ACLs.

q: An app must read messages from an Azure Storage queue using Entra ID. Which role?
opts: Storage Queue Data Message Processor (or Queue Data Reader)
Storage File Data SMB Share Reader
exp: Queue messages are data, so access needs a queue data role. Storage Queue Data Message Processor can peek, read and delete messages, and Storage Queue Data Reader can read them. Blob and file roles don't apply to queues, and Reader is a control-plane role.

q: What's the narrowest scope at which you can assign Storage Blob Data Reader?
exp: Blob data roles can be assigned down to the container scope (not individual blobs). Use ABAC conditions for finer control.

q: Which portal setting makes the portal use Entra ID instead of access keys when browsing blob data?
opts: Default to Microsoft Entra authorization in the Azure portal
exp: The storage account setting 'Default to Microsoft Entra authorization in the Azure portal' makes the portal use your Entra identity and data roles when browsing blobs, instead of the account key. The other settings are about encryption, Data Lake or anonymous access.

q: Which share-level role lets users read, write, and delete files over SMB, but not change NTFS permissions?
opts: Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor
Storage File Data SMB Share Reader
Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor
exp: Contributor = read/write/delete; Elevated Contributor can also modify NTFS ACLs; Reader = read only.

q: Administrators must change NTFS permissions on folders in an Azure file share. Which share-level role do they need?
opts: Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor
Storage File Data SMB Share Reader
exp: Changing NTFS permissions on files and folders needs the Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor role at share level. The ordinary Contributor role can read, write and delete but can't change ACLs, and Reader is read-only. Storage Blob Data Owner applies to blobs, not file shares.

q: All authenticated identities should get the same share-level permission without individual assignments. What do you use?
exp: A default share-level permission applies to all authenticated users when no specific role is assigned.

q: To enable on-premises AD DS authentication for Azure Files, the storage account must be:
opts: Joined/registered to the AD DS domain as a computer or service logon account (for example, with the AzFilesHybrid module)
exp: The storage account is represented in AD DS as an identity, usually set up with AzFilesHybrid's Join-AzStorageAccount.

q: Which identities must users have for AD DS authentication to Azure Files to work?
opts: Hybrid identities synced to Entra ID via Entra Connect
exp: With AD DS authentication, users sign in with their on-premises AD accounts, but share-level permissions are Azure RBAC roles, which need an Entra identity. So users must be hybrid identities synced from AD DS to Entra ID with Entra Connect. Cloud-only, guest and local accounts aren't in the on-premises domain.

q: Answer Yes or No about Azure Files access:
stmts: The storage account key can still mount a share even when identity-based auth is enabled
NTFS permissions alone are enough without any share-level permission
Azure Files supports identity-based auth over SMB
SAS tokens can be used to mount SMB shares
exp: The key works like a superuser; share-level permission is needed; SMB identity auth is supported; SAS works for REST access, not SMB mounts.

q: Security wants to make sure no container in an account can ever be set to public. Which account setting?
exp: Setting 'Allow Blob anonymous access' to Disabled on the storage account blocks anonymous access to every container, whatever each container's own setting is. Secure transfer, the firewall and soft delete don't control anonymous reads.

q: With the 'Container' anonymous access level, anonymous users can:
opts: Read blobs and list the blobs in the container
exp: The 'Container' anonymous access level lets anyone read blobs and list the blobs in the container. Anonymous users can never write or delete. The 'Blob' level allows reading without listing.

ctx: Storage account st1 has the firewall set to selected networks with SubnetA allowed. A user on VM1 in SubnetB uses a valid SAS.
q: Will the request succeed?
opts: Yes, a valid SAS always works
No, the firewall still blocks traffic from networks that aren't allowed
exp: The firewall is checked before the SAS. A request from SubnetB doesn't match the allowed network rule, so it's rejected even though the SAS token is valid. Authorisation (SAS, keys, Entra ID) and network rules are separate checks, and both must pass.

q: Which authorization method does Microsoft recommend for blob access from Azure-hosted apps?
opts: Microsoft Entra ID with managed identities
exp: Microsoft recommends Microsoft Entra ID authorisation with managed identities for apps running in Azure. There are no secrets to store or rotate, and RBAC data roles give least privilege. Account keys and SAS tokens embedded in code or configs can leak, and anonymous access gives no control at all.

q: Which TWO methods let you revoke access that was granted via SAS?
opts: Delete or modify the stored access policy the SAS references
Regenerate the account key that signed the SAS
exp: Revoke policy-based SAS through the policy; ad-hoc SAS through key rotation. (User delegation SAS can also be revoked by revoking the delegation keys.)

q: How do you invalidate all user delegation SAS tokens immediately?
opts: Revoke all user delegation keys for the account
exp: Revoking user delegation keys (az storage account revoke-delegation-keys) invalidates all user delegation SAS.

q: Which statement about CORS on a storage account is correct?
opts: CORS rules let browser apps from specific origins call storage endpoints
exp: Browsers block web pages from calling another domain unless that domain allows it with CORS. CORS rules on a storage account list the origins, methods and headers that may call its endpoints, so a web app on another domain can use storage from the browser. CORS isn't a firewall, an authorisation method or encryption.

q: Order the steps so that only VNet1/SubnetA can reach storage account st1:
items: Add a VNet rule for VNet1/SubnetA on st1
Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on SubnetA
Set st1 public network access to 'Enabled from selected networks'
Test access from a VM in SubnetA
exp: Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on SubnetA first, because a VNet rule needs it. Then switch the account to 'Enabled from selected networks' and add the VNet rule for VNet1/SubnetA. Finally test from a VM in that subnet. Doing it in this order avoids cutting off access before the rule exists.

q: Which feature allows specific Azure resource instances (for example, one Synapse workspace) through the storage firewall?
exp: Resource instance rules grant access to specific resource instances based on their managed identity.

q: Different containers in one storage account must be encrypted with different customer-managed keys. Which feature?
exp: Encryption scopes let different containers or blobs in the same storage account use different encryption keys, including different customer-managed keys. Infrastructure encryption adds a second layer for the whole account, and object replication and immutability aren't about keys.

q: Which identity does a storage account use to access the customer-managed key in Key Vault?
opts: A managed identity (system- or user-assigned) with key permissions
exp: The storage account authenticates to Key Vault with a managed identity that has the needed key permissions.

q: What happens to blob access if the customer-managed key is disabled in Key Vault?
opts: Data operations fail with 403 until the key is re-enabled
The account switches to Microsoft-managed keys
exp: With customer-managed keys, Azure Storage needs your key to decrypt data. If the key is disabled or access is revoked, reads and writes fail with 403 errors until it's re-enabled. Data isn't deleted, and the account doesn't quietly switch back to Microsoft-managed keys.

q: With customer-managed keys, which option lets Azure Storage automatically use the newest key version after rotation?
opts: Specify the key URI without a version (automatic key version updates)
exp: If you configure the key URI without a version, Azure Storage automatically starts using the newest version after you rotate the key in Key Vault. A fixed version stays on that version until you update the setting yourself.

ctx: st1: firewall = selected networks (SubnetA, office IP 203.0.113.10), shared key access disabled, public anonymous access disabled.
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: A VM in SubnetA with a managed identity holding Storage Blob Data Reader can read blobs
A user at the office using an account SAS can read blobs
An anonymous user on the internet can read a blob by URL
A user at the office with Storage Blob Data Reader can read blobs in the portal (Entra auth)
exp: Entra auth from allowed networks works; account SAS needs shared key auth, which is disabled; anonymous access is disabled; the office IP is allowed and Entra auth works.
